hints: Start at A - look for the tiny gap between two adjacent grey Schwann cells where the inner fibre is exposed.
Now follow B - trace the long thin fibre that runs inside the Schwann cells all the way from the large nucleated region to the synaptic knobs.
Finally look at C - focus on the large expanded region that contains the nucleus and gives off dendrites; this is the metabolic centre of the cell.
walkthrough:
Spot the Gaps in the Covering**
A points to the small uncovered gap between two Schwann cells. Myelin cannot form there, so ions can move and an action potential can be regenerated. That gap has a special name - the node of Ranvier.

Follow the Long Conducting Fibre**
B points to the central fibre enclosed by the Schwann cells. This is the axon, the long process that carries the action potential away from the cell body toward the terminals.

Identify the Control Centre**
C brackets the swollen part containing the nucleus with dendrites leading into it. This is the cell body or soma, where incoming signals are integrated and where most protein synthesis for the neurone occurs.
Final answer: A - node of Ranvier; B - axon; C - cell body (soma).

hints: Think of the order in a reflex arc - receptor to sensory neurone to relay neurone in the CNS, then what is the last neurone before the response happens?
Think about where that last message must go to cause a response - what two types of tissues carry out responses?
walkthrough:
Place the Motor Neurone in the Chain**
In a reflex arc the signal travels: receptor -> sensory neurone -> relay neurone in spinal cord or brain -> motor neurone. So the motor neurone is the outgoing link from the CNS. It carries action potentials away from the CNS.

Link to the Response**
The axon of the motor neurone ends at an effector. That is usually a muscle to contract or a gland to secrete. When the impulse arrives, the effector produces the rapid involuntary response.
Final answer: Transmits impulses / action potentials from sensory / relay / intermediate neurones in the CNS to effectors, muscles / glands, to bring about a response.

hints: Look again at Fig. 2.1 - what do the grey Schwann cells do around the axon and what layered covering does this produce?
Think about what that fatty covering does to ion movement across the axon membrane underneath it.
If ions cannot move under the covering, where along the axon can depolarisation and action potentials still occur?
Think about how jumping between those widely spaced points, about 1-3 mm apart, affects the speed compared with travelling along every part of the membrane.
walkthrough:
Build the Myelin Sheath**
The axon in Fig. 2.1 is wrapped many times by Schwann cells. Their membranes form a thick fatty layer called the myelin sheath. Think of it like plastic insulation around an electrical wire.

Insulate to Restrict Ion Flow**
Myelin is an electrical insulator. Where it covers the axon, $Na^+$ and $K^+$ cannot cross the membrane, so no depolarisation can happen there. This forces the signal to behave differently from an unmyelinated fibre.

Force Action Potentials to the Nodes**
The only exposed parts are the nodes of Ranvier, gaps like A. Voltage-gated channels are concentrated there, so action potentials are regenerated only at the nodes, which are 1-3 mm apart. Local circuits between a node and the next node are therefore long.

Jump for Speed - Saltatory Conduction**
Because depolarisation jumps from node to node instead of occurring at every point along the membrane, this is called saltatory conduction. It is much faster, about $50\times$ faster than unmyelinated conduction, reaching about $100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Final answer: Schwann cells wrap around the axon to form the myelin sheath; myelin insulates the axon preventing ion movement; depolarisation / action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier; longer local circuits form between nodes so impulses jump node to node by saltatory conduction, giving fast transmission, e.g. up to $100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

hints: Combine the two facts given - neurones up to 30 metres long in a huge animal - what problem would slow conduction cause for getting a muscle to move in time?
walkthrough:
Link Distance to Survival**
A blue whale is enormous and its motor neurones can be 30 m long. If impulses travelled slowly, the delay from CNS to tail or fin muscles would be too long. Fast saltatory conduction shortens that delay so the whale can move, feed or avoid danger quickly enough to survive.
Final answer: Very long neurones over a large body size, so fast conduction needed to respond / react to danger quickly.
